learning_outcomes.description: Evaluate the intersection of food science with nutrition science to justify your approach to the translation of nutrition science into dietetic practice
Recognise complexity and apply critical reasoning when analysing the impact of national and global Agri-food system at multiple levels of the food supply
Apply extensive understanding of nutrition and food sciences, and food sustainability to evaluate and justify practical information and recommendations for consumers
Explain and justify the role of traditional dietary patterns in a food system compared with ultra-processed foods

Work effectively within a student team to develop communication and process management skills by collaboratively modifying recipes for clients with varied medical/dietary conditions and integrating AI tools to solve nutrition and food science problems

assessments.task_description:
Students conduct hands-on dietary modifications in kitchen laboratory sessions, adapting recipes for specific dietary needs or health conditions. The assessment requires detailed documentation of ingredient substitutions, cooking methods, and their impact on nutritional content, taste, and texture. Students analyze the food science principles underlying their modifications and provide practical recommendations for clients, including preparation ease and cost considerations. The report includes comprehensive sections on aims, methods, results, analysis, and conclusions, with emphasis on translating nutrition science into practical dietary advice. This assessment develops critical skills in recipe modification, client-centred nutrition counselling, and understanding the intersection of food science with therapeutic nutrition practice. The Dietary Modification report outcomes will include comments on information that can be provided to clients about preparing modified recipes as well as links to planetary health.

assessments.assessment_title: AI Powered Food Systems Analysis Project
assessments.task_description:
Modern dietetic practice increasingly involves working within complex food systems where AI tools are becoming standard for product development, nutritional analysis, and consumer communication. This project develops your ability to leverage AI effectively while maintaining the critical thinking and evidence-based approach essential for professional practice. You will conduct a comprehensive analysis that simulates real-world scenarios where dietitians collaborate with food industry professionals to improve public health outcomes through product reformulation.

Use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) 

This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance.

A failure to reference generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct.

To pass this assessment, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of AI and MT tools.

learning_activities.topic:
Session 1: Intersection of Nutrition Science and Food Science

Workshop 1 introduces students to the overarching themes of the course and the systems-based approach that frames contemporary food and nutrition practice. Students explore how food science and nutrition science work together to influence the food supply, dietary recommendations and health outcomes, while becoming familiar with the course structure, practical components and assessment requirements. Through discussion and contemporary examples, students begin developing the critical thinking skills needed to translate food science into evidence-informed dietetic practice.

learning_activities.topic:
Session 2: Consumer Perspectives and Dietary Patterns

This workshop explores how dietary patterns have become central to contemporary nutrition science, shifting the focus from individual nutrients to the overall quality and complexity of the foods people eat. Students examine traditional dietary patterns, including the Mediterranean, Nordic, plant-based and planetary health diets, and evaluate the evidence underpinning their relationships with health and sustainability.

Students also critically explore the emergence of ultra-processed foods, food classification systems, and the broad range of social, cultural, economic and environmental factors that shape food choices. By considering dietary patterns within a food systems framework, students develop the critical reasoning skills needed to evaluate dietary recommendations, food policy and population health nutrition in contemporary dietetic practice.

learning_activities.topic:
Session 3: Food Systems 1

This workshop introduces food systems thinking as a framework for understanding how food is produced, processed, distributed, consumed and wasted, and how these interconnected processes influence human health, environmental sustainability, society and the economy. Students explore Australia's food system alongside global agri-food systems, examining the complexity of food production and the interactions between consumers, industry, policy and the environment. 

Drawing on contemporary examples, including the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, food waste, sustainability challenges and global food system transformation, students critically evaluate how food systems can be strengthened to improve health, resilience and equity. Throughout the workshop, students apply systems thinking to analyse real-world challenges and consider the evolving role of dietitians in creating sustainable food systems.

learning_activities.topic:
Session 4: Food Systems 2

Building on systems thinking introduced in the previous workshop, this session examines the complexity of national and global agri-food systems and the interconnected factors that influence food production, distribution, consumption and health outcomes. Students explore how environmental, economic, social and policy drivers interact across the food supply chain, recognising the cascading effects that changes in one part of the system can have on food availability, nutrition and population health. 

Using contemporary case studies—including global food supply chains, greenhouse gas emissions, biodiversity, food waste and ethical food production—students critically evaluate the sustainability challenges facing modern food systems. The workshop emphasises the role of nutrition and food science in developing evidence-informed, practical recommendations for consumers while balancing health, environmental sustainability and ethical considerations, preparing students to think beyond individual food choices towards systems-level solutions.
